**Min Cell Size** is set very low in your example. To minimize cascade shifts, you should set to a higher value (usually at least `0.1`). This means individual cascades will span a greater distance. GI won't look as detailed when up close, but it'll be less distracting in motion.

I've managed to add support for dynamic objects in HDDAGI, but it currently has a heavy impact on performance. I also added a setting to control how often the cascades are updated (every X frames). Does anyone have any ideas on how to improve this? https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/181b5e2b-eb11-43e3-8aaf-202acd8ff3a1

> Does anyone have any ideas on how to improve this?

When Update Interval is set above 1, stagger the cascade updates across frames to avoid frametime spikes. For example, if it's set to 5, update 20% of cascades every frame. You could use a random heuristic for this, or use a deterministic order like the cascade position (near/far away from the camera).

You could also perform dynamic updates less often (or even not at all) for far away cascades by adding a property, and focusing more on performing updates on cascades closer to the camera.

With this, I think a default value of 5 frames would perform well.

My tests have shown that HDDAGI has architectural flaws that are unlikely to be fixed. I added support for handling dynamic objects and pushed a commit, but it doesn't work as well as I'd like. Perhaps someone else will be able to refine this system in the future. Overall, I now understand why Juan Linietsky abandoned its development

If I remember correctly, the developers working on Radiance cascades found multiple solutions to this problem, though they introduced other minor problems. You can look into that. Using probes is why you get these issues; that's why I told Juan to use cascades instead of probes, because using cascades would be easier to find a solution to these issues, because probes are static by nature, so they will generate artifacts when making the scene dynamic, but with cascades, you can hide these imperfections.

He didn't want to say I was right due to his ego, but he just decided to leave the project, making up an excuse that he would resume the work due to not being able to find a complex solution to the radiance cascades shortcomings or to work with the developers on it, but I knew it was fundamentally impossible to make it work; it's mathematically impossible. Probe grids are sparse, and they don't pair well with a Hierarchical Grid, so you end up needing a denoiser, which makes the performance even worse, which was what he was also trying to do.

Check these out, you might get some ideas from them:

I've further improved the implementation of dynamic objects in HDDAGI. I would be very grateful if you could test it out and report any bugs or artifacts you find.

https://github.com/David-Zuloyan/godot/actions/runs/28739388175

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/63d165c2-086a-422c-8669-9fc12050289a **Testing project:** [test_hddagi_dynamic.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/29725033/test_hddagi_dynamic.zip) I tested https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/119869#issuecomment-4885979098, here's some feedback: - Dynamic objects work (CPUParticles3D and GPUParticles3D can even contribute to GI), but it's quite flickery when objects move. Even when objects don't move, it's not as stable as it could be. - Enabling TAA/FSR2 helps somewhat, as expected. - Increasing the number of frames to converge in the Project Settings helps the most. The default is 6; increasing it to 32 (a value similar to the current SDFGI) gets rid of most flickering. It does make light updates quite a bit slower, so maybe we should default to a middleground like 18 or 24. - If specific problem meshes could be ignored by HDDAGI (see below), this could be alleviated significantly by excluding these meshes from contributing GI (they'd still receive GI). - When dynamic objects are enabled, there will occasionally be stray indirect light from dynamic objects elsewhere in the scene. This can be seen at the end of the video below (the multicolored light comes from the particles that were seen earlier in the video): https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/9b675788-2188-449d-b72b-b51513ad7c97 - Dynamic objects should be disabled by default, as they have a performance impact even if there are no dynamic objects in the scene. - Meshes' global illumination modes are ignored, and are always treated as if they were set to **Static**. This means that dynamic objects can't be excluded from GI (when Dynamic Objects is disabled in the DynamicGI inspector), or when dynamic objects are enabled in HDDAGI, specific objects can't be configured to not contribute GI to reduce flickering. - The **DynamicGI > Light > Energy** property can be set to negative values in the inspector. This should be prevented using the `0,16,0.001,or_greater` property range hint. - Disabling **Filter > Probes** seems to act the same as disabling **Dynamic Objects > Objects** (it does not disable probe filtering, and disables dynamic objects instead). - Filter intensity should be hidden in the inspector when the respective filter is (probes/ambient/reflection) is disabled, using `_validate_property()`. As for reflection quality, keep in mind GI runs at half resolution (1/4th of the viewport pixel count) by default with this PR: Half resolution enabled | Half resolution disabled -|- | The reflection computations themselves are done at half the resolution of the GI buffer, which means that when half-resolution GI is enabled, reflections occur at quarter resolution (1/16th of the viewport pixel count). Diffuse GI is also affected by this, but it's not as noticeable unless you have a lot of thin geometry that is mostly indirectly lit. Since the half resolution GI project setting also affects VoxelGI, it may be preferable to disable it by default to avoid affecting visuals in existing projects and improve HDDAGI quality out of the box. This will make HDDAGI significantly more demanding on the GPU, but I think it's still within the expected bounds of real-time GI cost. All this feedback (except dynamic objects) also applies to this PR outside of @David-Zuloyan's fork.

SSIL and contact shadows serve different purposes:

- SSIL does not reuse probes from HDDAGI to do its work. This means it can work independently from HDDAGI (it works even with LightmapGI), but it's not as precise.
- Contact shadows only help reduce shadow peter-panning from shadow maps, and allow objects that have shadow casting disabled for performance reasons (such as grass) to cast shadows. They don't affect indirect lighting.

> * Contact shadows only help reduce shadow peter-panning from shadow maps, and allow objects that have shadow casting disabled for performance reasons (such as grass) to cast shadows. They don't affect indirect lighting.

Can we also implement a ray tracing path so we could trace it using the hardware-accelerated ray tracing cores? Also, what if we packed the ray results into a 3D grid of raw integers representing visibility bitmasks, mapped it to the probe grid, and stored it using spherical harmonics instead of using floating-point radial distances or depth maps inside their probe textures? This is just something to experiment with.

1. Instead of assigning a FORMAT_R16G16B16A16_SFLOAT to hold the visibility data, we could change the storage buffer format to map an unsigned integer grid FORMAT_R32_UINT, which would change the storage from a depth buffer to map an unsigned integer.

3. We could do a software bit-pack post-DDA hit, or after it traces light through the hierarchical voxel grid using HDDA, we could flip that bit with this if DDA ray reports an occlusion hit within our thickness threshold, which could mask the artifacts
visibility_grid[probe_idx] |= (1 << bin_id);

4. Then we can have the pixel look up its world-space position and sample the nearest bits from the 32-bit integer grid, and instead of running floating-point linear interpolations to guess visibility percentage, let's use the GPU's native bitwise functions. 
In Godot's GLSL backend, we can directly invoke hardware-accelerated execution such as this:
uint visible_sectors = 32 - bitCount(sampled_bitmask); 
float visibility_weight = float(visible_sectors) / 32.0;

[HDDAGI DDA Raymarch] ──► [Hit Voxel] ──► [Calculate Thickness] ──► [Pack into 32-bit Integer Grid] ──► [Sample 8 Closest Bits Map]  ──►  [Hardware bitCount Intrinsic]  ──► [Fragment Shader] 

We could then think about using a temporal or spatial blur filter after it; these mostly help the artifacts. Or we could go the restir routes, which would need a denoiser and spatial blur, which wouldn't be as performant. or the radiance cascades using surfel routes, which could alleviate the artifact, but at the cost of performance. Your choice.

Doom: The Dark Age inspired me, listening to their SIGGRAPH video, the only issue they got was stair-step angular pixelation, floating effect, and harsh shadow transitions or shadow ghosting, but no temporal artifacts whatsoever.

The Angular pixelation was fixed by using Angular Dithering. In their fragment shader, they rotate the light lookup direction using a screen-space blue noise texture before calculating the bit index. This instantly scatters the jagged lines into high-frequency grain, which can be cleanly smoothed away by the engine's Temporal Anti-Aliasing (TAA) pipeline.

The Floating effect was fixed using Depth-Dependent Normal Biasing. When the pixel shader samples the 3D bitmask texture, you pull the sample coordinate slightly inward along the surface's geometric normal vector, scaling the offset based on the camera's linear depth. This forces the grid to evaluate occlusion right at the point of contact, grounding objects tightly.

The harsh shadow transitions or shadow ghosting were fixed using Bilateral Screen-Space Filtering. They said not to let dynamic objects read directly from the slow-updating 3D bitmask volume. Instead, run a screen-space bilateral blur pass on the final lighting buffer. The filter compares the current frame's per-pixel object depth and vertex normals; if it detects a massive discontinuity (like a fast-moving demon or a moving elevator), it instantly rejects the cached temporal history and falls back to a fast screen-space approximation (like GTAO) for that frame until the 3D grid catches up.

Well, these were how the IdTech team fixed these issues. I also think it's the only viable method for a performance global illumination implementation, even the engine powering the new Assassin's Creed Black Flag Resynced uses it.

Thanks for the detailed writeup, appreciate the effort here.

Quick correction on the reference: DOOM: The Dark Ages' GI is hardware RTGI, not a software bitmask/HDDA scheme - it's actually why the game requires RT-capable hardware and can't run on older GPUs. So it's not the right example for "no temporal artifacts, only viable method on a software path." That said, the three fixes you listed (blue-noise angular dithering, depth-dependent normal bias, bilateral rejection falling back to a cheap screen-space term on fast motion) are real, standard techniques on their own, independent of that specific talk. The bilateral/screen-space fallback in particular lines up with what @MopanionStudios mentioned above about Juan's idea for a screen-space occlusion buffer to help with light leaking - might be worth digging into that angle specifically.

On the bitmask/SH idea: worth checking against what's actually here first. Occlusion is already `R16_UINT` (shared as `R4G4B4A4_UNORM_PACK16`), not a float format, so it's already compact. Radiance and occlusion are also already two separate octahedral textures (5x5 and 14x14), not a single depth/SH blob. The part I'd flag as a real open problem: bitwise-blending a 32-bit mask across the 8 nearest probes for trilinear sampling isn't well defined the way float interpolation is - you'd likely need `bitCount` per probe first, then blend the resulting floats anyway, which gives back most of the cost you're trying to avoid. And 32 bits is more than the current 16, not less, so it's not a memory win either as described.

A hardware RT path alongside HDDA is a reasonable ask, just a large separate scope (BLAS/TLAS management, a parallel shader path) - probably deserves its own issue/discussion rather than folding into this PR. For what it's worth, Anvil (AC Black Flag Resynced) ships exactly that split - hardware RTGI plus a software fallback for GPUs without RT support - so it's a proven pattern, just genuinely separate work from what's here.

I'm currently considering a few options, including a potential combination of HDDA and Radiance Cascades.

And most importantly, we all have to understand that we can't create a perfect global illumination system that simultaneously handles high-quality occlusion, specular reflections, and indirect lighting without relying on ray tracing. This is especially true considering that HDDA GI was essentially designed as a "good enough" GI system for older hardware without RT cores.
